blocks.x: New York and Symphony Hall Boston were tremendously successful. His films include Pennies from Heaven, Throwing Places, and Cabin in the Sky. He has recently gained additional international stature through his travels around the world as musical ambassador of goodwill. His artistry on the trumpet and his name as music. We'll meet Louis on the Cage set in Paris Blues in one minute.
All right, fix it. How do you like pancakes at your house? Plain? The picture, Paris Blues.

The gentlemen have taken a break. Here you see, as a matter of fact, a couch being carried out. And that'll give us a chance to talk to one of the country's top ambassadors of goodwill, Mr. Louis Armstrong. Ah, good to see you, Louis. Say, tell me this. How did you ever get the name Satchmo?

Oh, it was way back in the days of London when I was first around there in 1932. You arrived in Bristol. And the bell of the maker was strictly English. Uh-huh. He grabbed my hand and said, hello, Satchmo. I said, what you say, Daddy? You know, but I went to my trumpet player and I asked him, I said, my name is Satchmo. Why would he call me Satchmo? He said, because the man thought you had Mo mouth.
What are some of the other names that you've been called through the years? Well, you married, isn't it? No, no, I've been spared that. Well, you'll find out.
You'll find out all the names. My wife calls me, you know.
Yeah.

How'd you get started on the trumpet? Well, in the orphanage, when I was a little boy there, you know, we used to celebrate New Year's Eve. And I had my father's, 45, while this little kid across the street celebrating with a little six-shooter, you know. And die, die, die. And I pull up and you. And when I looked around, a detective had me. A policeman? A detective. Is that right? Yeah, he's a little high up on the horse. But he reached down and got you. He had me just the same.
And put you in the waif's home, huh?

Yeah. So, now, he treated me nice there. The first thing they gave me was a big plate of beans, you know. And I was playing hard to get for two days, you know. But after that third day, I could see that big plate of beans walking down a long table, you know, at the last supper. Anyway, when I got used to the beans, and they come as to showing me how to blow the bugle, and I was the official bugle of the institution. Yeah. They couldn't drill. They couldn't eat. They couldn't do nothing. They had to go to bed by my bugle and everything. Sometime I used to hold that mess call about five minutes later, and the cats would have killed me. How long were you there, Lou? Oh, about a year and a half. And my father, his boss, you know, how they can maneuver that. Yeah. Then Joe Oliver, they all stood for me. King Oliver. And then I used to run errands for King Oliver. Oh, and that's one of the greats. His wife used to cook them good old red beans and rice. And when he had his, I had my little bowl, too, you know. And I just grew right up on the Joe. Do you ever think you wanted to be anything else other than a musician? No. No. It's too late for her to think of when I play a typewriter and I write cats and things. But the horn is it.
You know, New Orleans is one of the most picturesque cities in America. You spent your childhood there. When you think back about New Orleans, do you ever want to, what comes through your mind?
Oh, well, the carnivals and the mardi gras were something to remember. Oh, yeah. We look forward to that. Everybody mass and the zoos, parade. Oh, boy. We used to go swimming at night, you know.
How about those funeral parades?

Yeah, the funerals. They take the body to the cemetery real slow. Everybody is serious, you know. And after the reverend, say ashes to ashes, dust to dust, you know what I mean? Yeah. They would kill the old brother Jones, his stomach arrest.
And then we go on back playing, didn't he ramble, oh, didn't he ramble.

And everybody jump in. Everybody's happy. And then when we get almost to the hall where they break up the parade, we put in them Saints Go Marching In. Oh, boy. And that's a traditional song. Yeah. When the Saints go. And everybody go to the saloon. And then...
Now, Storyville. Was Storyville everything that legend says it's like?

Yeah, I think so. But they put it in a nice way. Storyville, it used to be the red light district. It was. Yeah. But for modern eyes of the jazz and things, kids couldn't pick up on that. They didn't know it was Dolmott. So they just put Storyville from the musical end of it, see? And that's where jazz began, then? Was it going to drift up the Mississippi right up to Chicago? Right up to Mississippi on the levees and the plantations and all those melodies. And that rhythm, see? And before that, come to think of it, it was instilled in me that my great-grandfather, grandmother, way back there, they brought that rhythm from Africa to New Orleans. Oh, boy. Because I saw it when I went back. You ain't never seen so many rhythms. And different tribes, everyone had a different rhythm.

Well, that would be about our only true American music. Yeah, that's it. They brought it there. Now, those red beans and rice we were talking about, you had plenty of that. How do you like the French cooking over here? Well, that's the same.

French in New Orleans. You know, we got streets named Iberville, Bienville, and all the French people. And good cow and... You ate that? No, no, no. What is it? Stew turtle. Oh, no. Yeah. That's enough. No stew turtle. Oh, no. But they don't eat. They don't just throw him in there and cook him, you know. No? No. What do they do to him? Well, they take the little house off his back.
Louis Armstrong, a wonderful guy. He's been traveling all over the world as ambassador of goodwill for the United States of America. We'll hear more about that after this message.
A great new marble cake mix from Betty Crocker.

The star is Mr. Louis Armstrong. And recently, Louis traveled 60,000 miles in 45 days on behalf of the United States of America. Quite a record. Quite a guy. Louis, how did you happen to start in this field of yours being an ambassador of goodwill?

Well, I mean, we always loved each other and music in New Orleans. It comes from musicians appreciating each other. No matter where you meet him, what you say, man. Yeah. And your wife. Yeah. And your fans. A lot of them don't play music, but they know just what you're doing. And appreciation. That's why you can always sit in the crowd. And they all try to get backstage. Autographs. And I put in there, catch everybody, because I light them up and things like that.
And if you smile and are friendly to them, perhaps they get a better impression of the people in the United States. Yeah.

In the early days, I used to notice my leaders. They come on the job with a nice smile. They're going to have good music that night. Yeah. You know, everybody wake up, you know. Any of your friends ever criticize you for doing this? Well, no. They don't criticize me for doing that. But if I miss one of them notes, they don't fail to tell me. I mean, some of your friends criticize you for... Well, I call them my friends when they tell me the truth. Yeah. Yeah. They're friends.
You're concentrating a lot of your efforts on Africa.

Well, we're going back. We're going to... I can name a few spots, because it's a long list. But I know we're going to Dakar and Ethiopia and Egypt and a lot of little towns in Africa. Why are you going to Africa, Louis?

Well, I pray to all. No, I mean, do you feel that Africa now is coming into its own? Well... One state is being formed after another. Well, don't you think that, too? I do. Well, it's a strange subject. Do you feel that you can help them?
Well, I mean, in my way, if there's music the same as the Second World War, I got in bombers like soldiers did flying to camps to play music. I didn't charge for that.
Yeah. During these trips that you take, for example, well, wherever it is, Sweden, Africa, what are some of the questions that people ask you?

Well, what kind of food and what's happening in America, what they've cast during. There's a lot of trumpet players that are very good and perfect on instruments. We'd like to come to the States and show how good they can play. And I told them, I'll see Mr. Glazer. Maybe you can have some of them come over to go to school and come back and make bands and different things.
Now, how about the Russians?

You've been over there in Russia? I've been to Russia, yeah. I was slated to go to Russia with Ed Sullivan the week we played in Spileto. But I ate too much spaghetti one night and I'd stay there a week. You're going to go to Russia? I'll go anywhere. Just do it. Anywhere Joe Glazer sent me. I'll go. I mean, I just want to go to Holland.

Louie, do you feel that one of the reasons you're doing this is that America has been very good to you and you want to return? That's right. Back to return is when I just finished paying for my house. You better go back here. Yeah, I don't know another place. This is kind of a personal question, but what do you think are some of the faults that you have?
Well, I'll tell you when we come off the air.
I know one thing. You work mighty hard. We might stay on the air all day.
Well, we like that. We like our work and it's no problem.
How many hours a day do you sleep?
Well, I don't know, but if I can get four good ones, I'm straight with my laxative every night. I'm straight.
How many instruments do you play?

One. That's enough. You play that when you turn around. Now, do you prefer a live audience? Don't make no difference. You prefer it? Don't make no difference. Or when the man say, all on, and the leader say, one, two, and we're gone.

Now, when you were a little boy, beginning life, did you ever wish that you might have become maybe a doctor? No, he wasn't. What are some of the memories you have of New Orleans? I asked you that before, but I like that. Well, the childhood days were very nice.

I mean, we sold newspapers to use the things, and we used to go swimming and play baseball. We used to think like kids did. How do you compare your life here in France with your life in the United States? Well, I was a little older here. I mean, I thought you were talking about when I was a child.
Yes, but I mean now.

How do you compare my career? I was a kid. I was a kid. I don't do no more in the United States that my wife's with me, you know. Yeah. A young girl there, you know. You can figure it out yourself. Who all is in the Paris movies? Well, I know the stars. I kind of know all the people, you know. But I know Mr. Paul Newman and Sidney Poitier and Diane Cowell. And, well, I'm around them anyway. I mean, they're with them. They, you know, have a little fun, you know. Well, now, you've made movies in the United States. Oh, lots of movies.
How does the, how many working conditions? What?

This is our serious part of our interview here. Well, that's good. I'm just getting a laugh off. But, uh, see, the, the, the, you talking about the pictures in the, uh. Working here compared to working in the, uh.
Yeah, it's the same. When the man turned the camera, that's it. But aren't the hours different here?
No, there ain't no different. Hours is hours. I got to get up in the morning. See, that's just ready to sleep. But after the man grinded the camera, you know, chops fly everywhere.

And speaking of grinding cameras, I think they're just about ready to do that on Ferris Blues. Here in Ferris, it's been a pleasure, Louie. Okay. Thank you so much. Good luck to you. Thank you. The second half of here is Hollywood. We'll be coming your way from Ferris after this message.
Hello? Hi, honey. Your hands stay beautiful with...

segments.title: Introduction on the Paris Blues set
segments.summary: Host introduces Armstrong as goodwill ambassador from the Paris Blues set; an ad line is heard.

segments.title: How Armstrong got the name Satchmo
segments.summary: Armstrong says a man in England in 1932 greeted him as Satchmo, and his trumpet player explained the name came from his big mouth; talk turns to other names.

segments.title: Orphanage, the bugle, and running errands for King Oliver
segments.summary: He tells of being arrested for firing his father's pistol on New Year's Eve, the waif's home, learning the bugle, and growing up near King Oliver.

segments.title: Mardi Gras and funeral parades in New Orleans
segments.summary: He recalls carnivals, swimming at night and the slow funeral marches that turn lively with songs like Didn't He Ramble and The Saints.

segments.title: Storyville and the African roots of jazz rhythm
segments.summary: He describes Storyville as the red light district presented as the musical home of jazz, and says the rhythm came from Africa via the river.

segments.title: French food and street names in New Orleans
segments.summary: Light talk about red beans and rice, French street names and how stew turtle is prepared.

segments.title: Being an ambassador of goodwill and friendly audiences
segments.summary: He explains the goodwill tours as coming from musicians' appreciation of fans, recalls leaders smiling on the job, and says true friends tell him when he misses notes.

segments.title: Planned trips to Africa and what foreign audiences ask
segments.summary: He lists planned stops in Africa, compares it to playing for troops in the war, and says foreign trumpet players want to study in the States.

segments.title: Russia trip that fell through and returning America's kindness
segments.summary: He says he was slated to go to Russia with Ed Sullivan but missed it, will go anywhere Joe Glaser sends him, and feels he owes America.

segments.title: Work habits, sleep and playing one instrument
segments.summary: Short banter about his faults, working hard, sleeping four hours, playing only one instrument and not caring about live audiences.

segments.title: Childhood memories and the Paris Blues cast
segments.summary: He recalls selling newspapers and swimming as a child, then names Paul Newman, Sidney Poitier and Diahann Carroll as co-stars.

segments.title: Film working conditions and sign-off
segments.summary: He says the hours are the same in France as in US films, and the host closes the interview with an ad break.
